questions.q: Per this lesson, what should realistic sizing of compute and storage start from?
options: The expected load number already gathered in the requirements brief
Whichever instance size feels about right at the time
Whatever size was used on the previous unrelated project
The largest size available, regardless of expected load
questions.explain: Lesson 1's requirements brief already supplies the expected-load number that sizing actually depends on.

questions.q: What are the four steps of the realistic sizing loop described in this lesson?
options: Pick a reasonable baseline, deploy it, monitor real usage, then right-size based on that data
Guess a size, deploy it, and never check it again
Pick the largest available size, deploy it, and ignore monitoring entirely
Ask a competitor what size they use and copy it exactly
questions.explain: Sizing is a loop: a reasonable starting baseline, deployment, real monitoring, then an adjustment based on actual data.

questions.q: What real damage does over-provisioning 'just in case' cause, according to this lesson?
options: It quietly wastes budget every month on unused capacity with no corresponding benefit
It always causes an immediate outage
It automatically triggers a compliance violation
It has no downside at all, since more capacity is always better
questions.explain: Oversized infrastructure sits mostly unused while still costing money every billing cycle.

questions.q: What real damage does under-provisioning cause?
options: A real outage once traffic exceeds what the infrastructure can handle, often at the worst possible moment
A slight increase in the monthly bill with no other effect
It automatically resizes itself with zero downtime
It only affects storage cost, never compute performance
questions.explain: Under-provisioned infrastructure fails outright under real load rather than merely slowing down.

questions.q: Why does this lesson describe right-sizing as ongoing rather than a one-time decision?
options: Because real load changes over time, so treating the initial size as permanent repeats the same guessing mistake
Because cloud providers require a resize every single week by policy
Because monitoring data becomes inaccurate after the first day
Because right-sizing only matters during the initial planning meeting
questions.explain: A workload's real load can grow or shrink after launch, so sizing decisions need to be revisited against real monitoring data.
